newsitem.title: PERU: Aeroperu finds 55 bodies from Boeing 757 crash.
newsitem.headline: Aeroperu finds 55 bodies from Boeing 757 crash.

text.p: Peruvian airline Aeroperu said late on Friday rescuers had now found the corpses of 55 victims from its Boeing 757 that crashed into the Pacific ocean last month, killing all 70 on board.
Aeroperu officials said the rescue zone had been "substantially covered" in four weeks of searching, but operations would continue over the weekend to look for the remaining 15 bodies.
The airline has contracted the U.S. deep-sea specialist company Oceaneering Technologies to coordinate the search using frogmen and an underwater robot.
Aeroperu's flight 603 was carrying nine crew members and 61 passengers from 11 countries when it crashed into the sea north-west of the coastal capital of Lima soon after taking off for Chile.
Peru's Transport Minister Elsa Carrera said earlier this week the results of the analysis of the "black box" flight recorders being inspected by U.S. aviation experts would take about two months.

The Peruvian government has pinned the blame for the accident on technical faults in onboard computers, leaving pilot Eric Schreiber without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima after take-off.
But investigators from Aeroperu, Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board, have so far reserved judgment.
The 70 dead came from Chile, Peru, Mexico, Ecuador, the United States, Italy, Great Britain, New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.

The accident, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa. Since 1967, a total of 601 people have died in air crashes in Peru.
